query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating in-situ high-temperature imaging with real-time calorimetric measurements enables accurate and efficient determination of melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across diverse high-entropy alloy compositions.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or equilibrated high-entropy alloy samples exhibiting complex multicomponent phase structures.
generation.intervention: Heat the sample using an integrated furnace that simultaneously acquires high-resolution radiographic images and calorimetric data during controlled temperature ramps through the melting transition.
generation.conditions: High-temperature conditions spanning from below the solidus to above the liquidus; stepwise or continuous heating under controlled atmosphere (e.g., high vacuum or inert gas) to eliminate oxidation; synchronized imaging (e.g., neutron or equivalent high-penetration radiograph) and calorimetric data collection with temperature steps as fine as 20 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Dynamic observation of phase changes (e.g., onset of melting, phase separation or remixing) via high-resolution imaging that is directly time-correlated with calorimetric heat flow data.
generation.mechanism: The dual-modality system uses imaging to pinpoint the spatial and temporal onset of melting (tracking microstructural evolution) while calorimetric measurements supply quantitative energy input data. This combination allows extraction of thermodynamic parameters (melting temperature, latent heat, entropy change, associated volume change) by linking observed phase transformation events with the corresponding heat flow signatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Obtained melting temperatures and fusion thermodynamic parameters should agree within experimental error with known standards (or independently measured values) and show improved measurement efficiency, reducing experimental trial time significantly compared to sequential measurements. The method should be capable of capturing subtle microstructural transitions across the compositional variation inherent to high-entropy alloys.
generation.baseline: Traditional differential scanning calorimetry and separate high-temperature imaging techniques; these methods, when used independently, face limitations in either spatial resolution or speed and accuracy across the compositional space.
generation.boundary: The approach may be challenged in alloys with exceptionally high atomic number differences or compositional inhomogeneities that compromise imaging contrast or calibration of the calorimetric signal; it is applicable primarily in regimes where in-situ imaging offers clear phase contrast correlated to thermal events.
generation.uncertainty: While early studies (e.g., PMC8320920) indicate that in-situ imaging can capture dynamic phase changes, the quantitative linking between imaging signatures and thermodynamic parameters across the full compositional range of high-entropy alloys requires further validation. Instrument calibration, spatial resolution limits, and potential artefacts in data synchronization remain as areas of uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Select several high-entropy alloy compositions for which melting parameters have been reliably measured using traditional DSC and validated CALPHAD predictions. Subject these samples to the integrated measurement system while concurrently carrying out standard DSC tests. Compare the melting temperature, latent heat, and derived entropy and volume change from both methods.
measurements: High-resolution radiographic imaging data marking onset and progression of melting
Calorimetric heat flow curves during heating and cooling
Standard DSC measurements as independent reference data
Temperature calibration and synchronization logs between imaging and calorimetry
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the integrated method yields melting temperatures or latent heat values that consistently deviate beyond the combined experimental uncertainty (established via DSC and CALPHAD references) across a representative set of high-entropy alloys, or if discrepancies are observed between the imaging-detected phase transitions and corresponding calorimetric events, then the hypothesis is falsified.

AbstractReal-time neutron imaging was utilized to produce a movie-like series of radiographs for in-situ observation of the remixing of liquid state immiscibility that occurs in equiatomic CoCrCu with the addition of Ni. A previous neutron imaging study demonstrated that liquid state immiscibility can be observed in-situ for the equiatomic CoCrCu alloy. In this follow-up study, equiatomic buttons of CoCrCu were placed alongside small Ni buttons inside an alumina crucible in a high-temperature vacuum furnace. The mass of the Ni buttons was specifically selected such that when melted in the same crucible as the CoCrCu buttons, the overall composition would become equiatomic CoCrCuNi. Neutron imaging was simultaneously carried out to capture 10 radiographs in 20 °C steps from 1000 °C to 1500 °C and back down to 1000 °C. This, in turn, produced a movie-like series of radiographs that allow for the observation of the buttons melting, the transition from immiscible to miscible as Ni is alloyed into the CoCrCu system, and solidification. decision.trend: Early work in high-entropy alloys mainly relied on traditional calorimetric techniques and computational phase diagram calculations. These approaches either provided isolated insights or required extensive, time-consuming validation, and they struggled when extended across the compositional space of high-entropy alloys. Recent advances, such as the use of in-situ neutron imaging to capture dynamic melting behavior (as seen in PMC8320920), have demonstrated that real‐time observation of phase transitions is feasible. However, these imaging studies have focused on phase mixing and remelting phenomena rather than delivering a unified, quantitative determination of all fusion thermodynamic parameters.
decision.unsolved: No existing method offers a unified and validated approach to accurately and efficiently determine melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the broad compositional variability of high-entropy alloys. The decisive validation that would disprove a proposed approach — namely, an independent measurement that clearly differentiates between genuine phase-transition phenomena and experimental artefacts — is still lacking.
decision.lever: integrated in-situ high-temperature imaging coupled with real-time calorimetric measurement
decision.why: Given the incremental progress from isolated calorimetry and computational predictions to in-situ imaging techniques, the logical next step is to combine these approaches. An integrated setup that simultaneously captures high-resolution radiographic signatures of melting with real-time calorimetric data could quantitatively link observable phase transitions with accurate thermodynamic measurements. This would directly address the need for efficiency and accuracy across varied high-entropy alloy compositions and provide a decisive experimental validation capability by comparing independent datasets.
